coherence.reasons: Both run the same sound logic: market, Option A economics, Option B failure, Japan, then the plan. X puts all three options against every board constraint on one page early, and its executive summary names the two trade-offs (the $40M miss and the ACoS-dependent payback), which the later sections then support one by one. Y's governing thought is arguably sharper because it carries the payback condition, and its sections map cleanly to the key questions. But Y's option-versus-constraint synthesis arrives late, and its ACoS ceiling is never fixed at one number across the summary, risk table and scorecard. X has a small inconsistency of its own (repeat guardrail at 29% in the launch plan, 31% in the retail gate).

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation: Amazon-led with gates, retail rejected, Japan deferred, ambition reset. X weighs the alternatives more fully. It prices the Japan trade-off (about $19M of 2030 revenue forgone against roughly $4M of cash downside) and concedes the Head of Japan is right on safety. It stress-tests B across no-halo, 2.6 units and 32% ACoS cases, and shows B would need a 3.1x halo to pay back. Its controls are concrete: a $4M envelope with board approval beyond it, and a rule to slow paid growth if ACoS exceeds 30% for two quarters. It also notes that a full-cost national retail launch in 2029 would itself break payback, so retail must be resized. Y's Japan comparison rests mainly on revenue size and market growth, and its ad-cost ceiling and cash envelope are named but not quantified as decision rules. Y's test-doors-first idea with a 4.0 sell-through check is a good addition.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key's numbers accurately: $10.73 and $4.01 Amazon contribution, $7.55 retail, B peak of $20.8M, group margin 4.5%, A at +2.4 / +0.4 / -2.3 by ACoS, break-even 28.6%, and tariff cases. Both handle the $5.2B figure, the correlation memo, the awareness bands and the small competitor sample correctly. X adds more: break-even ACoS under the tariff (26.9%), volume sensitivities, the 38% ACoS case, the slowing of pilot month-on-month growth, and a list of modelling choices that flatter B. Y shows its break-even derivation transparently and has a useful retail break-even of about 32 units per door per week. Y slightly overclaims with "Demand is proven" and uses single-year 16.1% growth where a CAGR would be fairer. X's "payback is likely on planning inputs" is a little generous given the 32% benchmark, though it is flagged as at risk throughout.

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's Amazon-first sequence and add conditions, as the key expects. Both raise the awareness trigger from 15% to 20% using the sell-through bands and the 4.0 delisting bar, and both make payback conditional on ACoS and reset the $40M ambition. X goes further on the hypothesis itself: it qualifies the $10M sales gate with ACoS at or below 28%, adds a repeat gate and a self-funding retail-economics gate, replaces the fixed 2029 date with an end-2028 gate decision, and shows the retail step would break payback at full cost. Y keeps the $10M gate as is, but adds test doors first and a 4.0 units sell-through check, which is also a sensible refinement.

overall.reasons: The two documents reach the same defensible conclusion from essentially the same correct model. X serves the board better in less space. It gives a one-page view of the options against the constraints, a quantified Japan trade-off, a fuller stress test of B, and tariff-adjusted break-evens. It also gives explicit decision rules (the $4M envelope, ACoS triggers, multi-part retail gates) and states plainly the risk the board accepts. Y is solid and transparent in its derivations, and its retail break-even and test-door ideas are useful. But its controls are less specific and its weighing of the alternatives is thinner.
